title: Count Equal Value Pairs
description:
# Count Equal Value Pairs

Given an integer array `nums`, count every pair of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] == nums[j]`.

Pairs are counted by index, not by distinct value. For example, three equal values at different indices form three pairs.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,1,1,3]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** The equal-value index pairs are `(0,3)`, `(0,4)`, `(3,4)`, and `(2,5)`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,1,1,1]
**Output:** 6
**Explanation:** Four equal values form `4 * 3 / 2 = 6` index pairs.

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= nums.length <= 10^5`
*   `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
*   The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

solutions.name: Online Frequency Counting
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the array from left to right and keep a frequency map of values that have already appeared. When the current value `x` is seen, every previous `x` forms one new pair with the current index. Add the current frequency to the answer, then increment the frequency.

## Key Insight

The kth occurrence of a value creates exactly `k - 1` new index pairs. Counting pairs at the moment the right endpoint arrives turns the pair formula into a one-pass update.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public int countEqualPairs(int[] nums) { Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>(); int pairs = 0; for (int x : nums) { pairs += seen.getOrDefault(x, 0); seen.put(x, seen.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1); } return pairs; } }

solutions.name: Frequency Table Then Combinations
solutions.description:
## Approach

First build a frequency table for every value in `nums`. Then process each frequency `m` independently and add `m * (m - 1) / 2`, the number of ways to choose two indices that hold that value.

## Key Insight

Pairs from different values never interact. Once the array is grouped by value, the problem becomes a sum of combinations, one combination count for each group.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public int countEqualPairs(int[] nums) { Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>(); for (int x : nums) { counts.put(x, counts.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1); } int pairs = 0; for (int count : counts.values()) { pairs += count * (count - 1) / 2; } return pairs; } }

solutions.name: Sort and Count Runs
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the array so equal values become adjacent. Walk through each run of the same value. If a run has length `m`, add `m * (m - 1) / 2` pairs before moving to the next run.

## Key Insight

Sorting changes the order of indices, but it does not change how many times each value appears. Runs in sorted order are another way to expose the same value groups that the hash table stores explicitly.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
solutions.code: class Solution { public int countEqualPairs(int[] nums) { Arrays.sort(nums); int pairs = 0; int i = 0; while (i < nums.length) { int j = i + 1; while (j < nums.length && nums[j] == nums[i]) { j++; } int count = j - i; pairs += count * (count - 1) / 2; i = j; } return pairs; } }

solutions.name: Nested Pair Scan Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use two nested loops to enumerate every index pair `(i, j)` where `i < j`. Count the pair only when `nums[i] == nums[j]`.

## Key Insight

This is the definition written directly as code. It is too slow for large inputs, but it is the clearest baseline for understanding what the frequency and sorting solutions are aggregating.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
solutions.code: class Solution { public int countEqualPairs(int[] nums) { int pairs = 0; for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) { if (nums[i] == nums[j]) { pairs++; } } } return pairs; } }
